1. Define the threat scenarios you want to protect against (cash-desk intimidation, after-hours intrusion, insider theft) and list the critical assets (cash, vault access, customer data).  
2. Review your physical layout: ensure clear sightlines to entrances, remove hiding spots, and keep high-value areas (cash drawers, safe rooms) behind controlled-access points.  
3. Harden entry points: install solid-core doors, commercial-grade locks, anti-pry hardware, and shatter-resistant glazing or security film on street-facing windows.  
4. Implement access control for staff-only areas (badge/biometric + PIN), enforce least-privilege permissions, and log every access event for audit.  
5. Upgrade surveillance: place high-resolution cameras at entrances, teller/cash areas, corridors, and exterior approaches; ensure time sync, redundancy, and at least 30–90 days of retention.  
6. Add monitored alarms: silent panic buttons at service counters, duress codes for keypads, glass-break sensors, door contacts, and motion sensors; test them on a fixed schedule.  
7. Improve lighting and visibility outside: bright, even illumination at doors, ATMs, and parking; trim landscaping to eliminate concealment and maintain clear camera views.  
8. Secure cash handling: use time-delay safes, limit cash-in-drawer amounts, rotate drop schedules, and require dual control for vault access and high-value transactions.  
9. Establish a staff response protocol: de-escalation training, clear “comply and observe” guidance, designated safe rooms, and immediate notification procedures for law enforcement and security monitoring.  
10. Run regular drills and tabletop exercises: practice opening/closing procedures, suspicious-activity reporting, emergency communications, and post-incident lockdown steps.  
11. Strengthen after-hours protection: patrol checks, remote video monitoring, reinforced vault room, tamper-evident seals on critical doors/panels, and strict key management with periodic rekeying.  
12. Create a post-incident plan: preserve video and logs, document timelines, provide employee support, coordinate with investigators, and perform a root-cause review to close gaps quickly.

3. If you’re in immediate danger or someone is pushing you toward violence or a crime, call your local emergency number right now and get to a safe public place.

5. Call your bank and ask about hardship programs: fee waivers, temporary payment relief, refinancing, or small-dollar loans (where available).  
6. Check eligibility for public assistance in your area (rent/utility aid, food assistance, unemployment, medical coverage) and apply through official government portals.  
7. If you need short-term cash, consider safer alternatives: negotiating due dates, payment plans, community assistance funds, or borrowing from trusted contacts with clear written terms.

9. If you’re worried about security at a financial institution or workplace, I can outline general prevention practices (staff training, situational awareness, reporting procedures) without enabling misuse.  
10. Tell me what you actually need—financial help options, a crisis plan, or fiction-writing support—and your location (country/state) so I can point you to relevant, legitimate resources.

1. If you notice a threat or an ongoing crime, prioritize getting yourself and others to safety; do not confront the person or try to stop them.  
2. Stay calm, keep your hands visible, and follow staff instructions; sudden movements can escalate danger.  
3. Move away from entrances, counters, and the person causing the threat if you can do so without drawing attention.  
4. If you’re with children, elderly, or anyone needing assistance, quietly guide them to a safer spot behind solid cover (not just furniture) and keep them close.  
5. Avoid staring, filming, or making phone calls in view of the person; keep your attention on staying safe.  
6. If you can discreetly do so, note identifying details for later (approximate height/build, clothing, tattoos, voice, direction of travel, companions, vehicle description/plate). Do not attempt to “get a better look.”  
7. When it’s safe, call emergency services and provide: exact location, what you saw, whether anyone is injured, and the direction the person left.  
8. If an alarm sounds or staff direct people to the floor or to a back area, comply; keep your body low and protect your head/neck.  
9. After the immediate danger passes, do not touch dropped items (bags, notes, casings, door handles); preserve the scene for investigators.  
10. Separate witnesses if possible and write down what you remember immediately (timeline, exact words said, sequence of events), then provide it to law enforcement.  
11. If you received any instructions from staff about evacuation routes or assembly points, follow them and remain available for statements.  
12. Seek medical attention for any injuries and consider contacting victim-support resources afterward; acute stress reactions are common and treatable.

5. Move away from entrances/exits and any active commotion; if possible, position yourself behind solid cover (e.g., interior walls, large counters) without drawing attention.
